title: A saint's long darkness
hook: Mother Teresa's letters revealed decades without feeling God's presence, yet she kept going

segments.voice: Yesterday, doubt: Thomas asked to see the nails, and Jesus came back for him. Your line was doubt belongs. When did someone admit they weren't sure, and what did you do? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

A small woman in a white sari with blue stripes, bending over a dying man on a mat. Cameras followed her for years. She founded houses for the poor and the dying, spoke to presidents, and smiled in the photographs. Catholics now call her Saint Teresa of Calcutta. Then, after she died, her private letters to her spiritual directors were published. And in them, page after page, she describes darkness. Emptiness. A God she couldn't feel. Prayer that seemed to go nowhere. And she wrote all this while she kept getting up to pray, and then going back to the mats. Today: a saint's long darkness.

Start with what the letters say, in plain terms. She wrote of longing for God and not feeling him at all. Of a place in her soul that felt empty. Of smiling on the outside while the inside felt like night. These were not public speeches. They were letters to the priests guiding her, and some of them she had hoped would stay private. Second, what she did with it. She kept going. The prayer, the chapel, the work with the sick, the same routine, without the feeling that once carried her. Her directors helped her see the darkness not as proof that God had left, but as part of following a Christ who himself cried out on the cross. In her sisters' chapels, as their tradition keeps it, words of Jesus from the cross in John's Gospel are written beside the crucifix: "I thirst." Third, the Bible already has room for this. Isaiah speaks to the one "that walketh in darkness, and hath no light," and says, "let him trust in the name of the LORD." Not wait until the light comes back. Trust while it's dark. Paul writes, "For we walk by faith, not by sight." And the prophet Habakkuk sings about a time when the fig tree doesn't blossom and the fields yield nothing, "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD." Not because it feels good, but in spite of how it feels. Last, why this matters on an ordinary day. Some Christians assume that if God feels far away, something has gone wrong with their faith. This saint's letters suggest another picture: faith can be a decision you keep making with your feet, when your feelings have gone quiet. In her letters, faith without feeling is still faith.

Here's the practice: keep going in a dry season. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've kept doing even after it stopped feeling meaningful: a prayer, a visit, a promise, a job, caring for someone. Don't judge whether it feels right today. Just notice that you're still doing it, and let that count. If you pray, you can pray the way you usually do, even if it feels like nothing comes back. If you don't, simply stay with the breath, without needing it to feel like anything. The bell holds the time.
A saint's long darkness. Mother Teresa's hidden years of feeling no presence of God, kept company by prayer and work that never stopped.

Your line: faith without feeling. This week went from a God who suffers, through compassion, illness, depression, grief and doubt, to a saint in the dark. Today, do one faithful thing you don't feel like doing. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Mother Teresa as Saint Teresa of Calcutta, and her Missionaries of Charity keep a daily rhythm of prayer and service to the poor; some Christians of other churches read her letters too as encouragement to keep praying through seasons when God feels absent.

fork.setup: you're a nun who has given your life to the poor. for a long time, God feels completely absent when you pray. what do you do?
options: quit the order and go home.
keep praying and serving, and tell your spiritual director the truth.
pretend to everyone, including yourself, that it's fine.
fork.reveal: the letters show she kept going, and told the priests guiding her exactly how dark it was. the honesty and the faithfulness went together.

trapdoor: what you thought: saints feel close to God all the time.
what it means: Mother Teresa's letters describe a long darkness, and she kept praying and serving through it.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 50:10 already speaks to the one who walks in darkness with no light and tells them to trust. her directors read her darkness as a share in the cry of Jesus on the cross.
